know, "Speakers, don't say things like good afternoon because it puts like a timestamp on your talk. This doesn't make any sense when people watch it on
the internet 2 months later." So, for the web team, if you want to cut here, I'll start over. So, without further ado, thank you to
the teams at the Algorand Foundation and We Are Developers for putting all this together. It takes an incredible amount of work by a lot of people to make these
events happen. So, a small round of applause for everybody who puts on these productions. It's really incredible. My name is Brian Whippo. Uh like to build real stuff at the Algorand
Foundation, and today I want to talk to you about an HTTP status code 200 OK. But, payment settled, resource delivered is probably not what you thought it
meant, but we'll work our way up to that. Last year, I was on stage at We Are Developers and I gave a talk called 402
uh payment required. And the premise then was a bit theoretical. This idea that the agentic economy was going to emerge. People using autonomous AI
agents were going to use them to start buying and selling things. Now, this is rather concrete, and we're going to talk about how that's played out over the
past year. So, my opening premise today is that autonomous AI agents are here. This is real. It's very concrete, and they need digital payments. They need to
be able to buy and sell things. And there's a few key requirements. One is that they need to be able to settle their transactions atomically, so delivering
the resource at the same time that they get paid. This all needs to be programmable, like observable, verifiable etc. Uh the settlement has to be immediately
final. Can't be rolled back. You can't wait 2 days for a payment to go through for your AI agent. That just doesn't work on the time frames in which we
work. And all of this has to be permissionless. Not every transaction needs to have a verified buyer. Sometimes an AI agent needs to go out
and ask a question, get a resource, you know, upload data, access a data set, something like this. And the bottom line is that stable coins on blockchain
uniquely enable agentic commerce. So, I mentioned 402 payment required. As a refresher, if you're not familiar with this status code, HTTP cat can illustrate this for us.
He's loving this pile of money. And if you're a dog person, we have the HTTP status of dogs equivalent. He seems pretty relaxed, but he is covered in
money. To really talk about what 402 means, we go way back in history. Tim Berners-Lee sort of invented the World Wide Web, proposed this in 1993.
This is over 30 years ago. This idea that there would be a specification to charge someone over the internet using this low-level protocol. We've come a long way since then,
though. But, it's still reserved for future use. Last year, I issued a call to action to people to say, "Now is the time to get together and
think about how we can put this unused, undefined status code into practice." And in the last year, there's been an enormous amount of progress.
MDN explains that 402 payment required is basically a non-standard response. We want to get to the point where it's standard. And it was intended to enable
digital payments, maybe micro payment systems and and enable through web primitive technologies the ability to make these exchanges over HTTP. But, still no standard use or convention exists. And
it's not yet supported in browsers. This is an interesting point I'll come back to. Last year, the idea that you could use a protocol
called X402 had just emerged right before the conference. And it was led at the time by Coinbase and it was a very web 3 thing. It was coming out of the
crypto industry, the ability to submit a blockchain transaction to pay for a resource over the internet. But that's matured quite a bit. Now this sits under
the X402 Foundation. So it sits in a more neutral organization. It's actually under the Linux Foundation projects, which gives it quite a bit of
credibility. They describe it as an open neutral standard for internet native payments. And then making a reference to a comment that someone made years ago, it
absolves the internet's original sin by natively making payments possible between clients and servers. And their one-liner to illustrate how this works is a bit of middleware that you can wrap
around an endpoint and say, "If you want to get the weather from my endpoint, I will tell you what networks and payment schemes I will accept before I give you
the response." So, I mentioned that this is concrete. This is real. This is live in production. It's not theoretical anymore. X402 .org keeps track of the production
volume going on. So this is just the last month, 75 million transactions, almost 25 million dollars worth of volume, and nearly 100,000 buyers. But
the interesting thing here is I mentioned this protocol is not supported in any browsers at the moment. So if you read between the lines, all of this
activity is presumably being driven by AI agents, right? Humans are not using their browsers to do this. This is all autonomous AI agents doing all sorts of
experimental things and playing around with the protocol, but it's doing real volume, and exchanging real money. So, I want to talk a little bit about
how this works. X402 takes the client-server model, and extends it a little bit. You still have the client. In this case, the client sends a request, and they include a
payment along with that request to receive the resource. The resource server can do one of two things. It can deliver the resource if it was appropriately paid for, or it can
say, "Nope, 402, payment required." The third role that is introduced in X402 is this idea of a facilitator. This is the interface with blockchains, where
the stablecoin payments are submitted and confirmed. So, the facilitator has a special role here to verify and settle these payments on a chain. Since last year, when this was first
introduced as a much simpler standard, it's actually now in version two of its life, and a lot of feedback from the community led to expansions of what you
can do with X402. One expansion of the capabilities is the way that you can pay for things. There's three methods in the specifications. The first is an exact
payment. I want some resource. It costs 1 euro cent. I pay the cent. I get the resource. It's all exact. Another way you can do this though,
which may resonate with us as users of AI, is this concept of up to. Maybe I want to pay up to a dollar for the
tokens I'm about to burn through, or the CPU I'm about to use, or something like that. And so, you can issue a payment up
to some amount, and the seller will only charge you for what you used, and the transaction will only clear for the amount that you use.
And then finally, for high-volume, high-frequency cases, sometimes it might not make sense to make a payment for every single resource. That's okay. You can also make batch payments, where you
authorize a payment for each resource individually, but only settle them later in batches. I'm going to talk through the X402 workflow first with a really simple
example, and then we're going to go down into a little bit more detail. Uh this is very high level. We're going to assume, as we do, that the client on
the left is an AI agent, and the API server on the right is the server in our uh list of roles. The AI agent requests the data to the
server, and the server says, "You haven't paid me yet. 402 payment required." Now the client can essentially resubmit the request, and they bundle with the server request a
signed transaction, a stablecoin payment to the server to the address that they're expecting the payment to. And then that blockchain payment gets verified that it's what the server
expected and settled, and the data is returned. And now you have sort of the the complete flow. Pretty straightforward. Let's dive in. The real flow is a little bit more
complex. This is the whole sequence diagram. It's a bit small. I will zoom in on this, so you can take a picture when I get to the
zoomed-in slides. Uh but this shows the the whole flow with all of the roles. And on the right, Algorand is the blockchain being used in
this example. So, the beginning of the workflow is familiar. The client sends the request across. We just saw this. And the resource server responds, "402 payment
required. And here are my requirements. I want to be paid on this chain. I want to be paid in this stablecoin, like USDC or a Euro money token, or whatever the
server wants to accept." And then the client goes and constructs a group of transactions. It could be multiple. Signs them with a wallet. And if your
agent doesn't have a wallet, that's probably something you should be thinking about, and you can come talk to us at the Algorand booth. And then when the client responds back
to the server, it uses a special header. So, it includes a payment signature header in that request when it goes back. And then, the resource server can
look at that and say, "Is this what I expect? Am I getting a payment for the resource I'm about to serve?" And we'll keep going.
At this point, the resource server asks the facilitator to check that the payment is actually going to succeed. So, what's happening here is there's a
check for the fee on the transaction cuz blockchain transactions charge fees. And in some cases, the facilitator can sponsor the fees. So, the buyer doesn't
even have to worry about that. They can just make a stablecoin payment. They don't have to think about the gas fee that it costs to make that payment. They
can just do it, and the facilitator can cover it. So, that's part of the model. And then, the facilitator will simulate that payment, make sure everything about

the transaction will evaluate successfully, and return the result. And then, resource server is like, "Wonderful. I see that that that simulation returned successfully, and I can request this transaction now
be submitted to the chain to be settled." And at this point, the facilitator will go back to Algorand. They'll submit this payment group, wait for the very next
block to be produced, and if it succeeds, then that payment has instantly settled. You don't have to wait any longer on Algorand. There's no
additional confirmations needed. It's a one-block or single-slot transaction finality. And so, at the bottom of this diagram, the facilitator reports back to the resource server the settlement was
successful, and the resource server says, "200 OK. Here's your resource." And this is the essence of the talk, right? 200 OK, payment settled, resource delivered. This is a little
[snorts] bit of a new paradigm. We got the 200 OK. HTTP cat doesn't seem particularly happy about this, but HTTP status dog is very happy about
this. So, he's thrilled. He's just basking in English ivy. He's loving the time of his life. Just to complete the total workflow, these are the failure scenarios. So, if
for some reason the original payment transaction that was submitted was not what the server expected, or if when it was simulated by the facilitator, it did
not evaluate successfully, or if the actual payment failed for some reason, some state has changed, these are all failure scenarios that revert right back
to 402 payment required, and then the workflow could basically start over and the client could try again. So, I mentioned last year I issued sort of a call to action
because the X402 protocol has matured quite a bit. The workflow that I just stepped through, it works, it's live, people are using it with real money in production.
But, the HTTP 402 status code is still not official. It's not supported by browsers. There's more work to do here. So, I wanted to link to the X402
Foundation's GitHub repo. Uh they maintain all the code, all the docs, specifications, etc. And the best way to push these things forward is for
as many people as possible to build real stuff for your businesses and for yourselves that solves a diverse set of problems. And together, we can form a
great standard for this new native capability for the web. One way that uh this is playing out and something that you can play with is
last week, Cloudflare announced what they call the monetization gateway. So, this is a productionized service with usage-based pricing. Um it's in it's intended to enable a different
business model for sites that have historically only been ad driven. But, for AI agents, they're not looking at ads, right? They're not clicking on ads
for sure, but you can serve resources through their gateway and charge for them. The payments are peer-to-peer, so for a lot of businesses, this simplifies
accounting invoicing billing things like this, as well as the fees that are required when you use third-party payment processors and intermediaries. Uh and in this gateway, the payments
settle in stablecoins on blockchain using X402. Uh this is their diagram of how it works. It looks very similar to my diagram. The agent on the left sends a
request. This should look very familiar, except this time they have a business abstraction wrapped around it, um but the process is fundamentally the same.
Um what they call out here that I mentioned earlier is that the agent is using its agent wallet to make that payment. So, I would be remiss if I did not convey
that Algorand is ready for agentic commerce. Um I want to leave you with the understanding that although blockchains have not always had this reputation collectively, Algorand
can handle extreme scale up to 10,000 transactions per second. We've never had any downtime since 2019, which is absolutely remarkable. Um we also have built-in capabilities
that make doing this in a compliant way easier. Uh the tokens on our chain have built-in freezing and clawback capabilities, and there are MiCA-compliant money tokens in Europe.
Uh one is issued by a company called Quantoz with a Z at the end. Uh and we are ready for the autonomous agentic systems that I described because
you can settle these transactions instantly, and if something does go wrong, the failure to submit a transaction doesn't cost anything. So, you you and
your agent are not out any money. So, I invite you to have a play around with this to try to solve a problem. Uh
we have a workshop tomorrow afternoon in the City Cube, upstairs on the third floor in room M8. Two of my colleagues, Jordan Bronson and Sergiyen Kenny, are
going to be teaching a 2-hour hands-on keyboard workshop building the Algorand economy with X402 and stable coins. This QR goes to the event page in the World
Congress app, so you can scan that and register. There may be a wait list, but sign up for the wait list anyway. Sometimes people don't show up and we
can still get you into the room. So, I still have a little bit of time. Actually, the timer is not going, but I have I think I have a little bit of
time. Um there's one more thing that I want to convey, which is Algorand is not just ready for Algorand commerce, but there's another frontier.
At the moment, many of the technologies that we use and that our applications depend on, including blockchains, but also low-level soft TLS, HTTPS, pass
keys, SSH keys, uh the chip cards you use to pay for things, SIM cards in cell phones, all of this rests upon elliptic curve cryptography.
And Algorand as a blockchain, the accounts and the signatures that you use are derived from Edwards curve, uh ED25519 uh accounts. Uh so, a private public key pair.
And this is at risk. There's a few people here today giving talks about quantum computing, advances in hardware, and how to program these things. And the advancement of
this technology has shocked a lot of people. Earlier this year in March, uh a notable example was Google published a research paper in which they said,
"We've looked long and hard at how to implement Shor's algorithm on a quantum computer." Shor's algorithm essentially breaks elliptic curve cryptography because it can factor these very large numbers
involved, and it makes math that's essentially impossible to do in a reasonable amount of time on a classical computer very fast to do on a quantum
computer. So, by their estimation of how many qubits it's going to take in a quantum computer to break elliptic curve cryptography, their recommendation is
now everyone needs to migrate to post-quantum cryptography by 2029. That's not very far away. So, I also want to convey one more thing. Algorand is ready for this post-quantum
future. Although our chain was founded on the Edwards curve elliptic curve, uh we have been working since 2022 to incorporate lattice-based cryptography, in this case
the Falcon digital signature scheme, into our blockchain. We started with signatures over the history of the chain so that it could not be tampered with by
someone with a quantum computer. Uh we currently have smart contract accounts that are secured by these Falcon 1024 signatures, and we will soon have native accounts protected by these
uh private keys. And we have a roadmap through 2027 to build a number of cryptographic primitives to upgrade the entire chain and all the things you need
to do to interact with a blockchain to use these post-quantum signature schemes. Things like hybrid accounts that blends together the security of, say, an Edwards private key and that
curve, as well as a Falcon key and its lattice, uh multi-signature accounts, the ability to do these signatures on hardware devices, and we're building our blockchain in a
way that it will be crypto-agile. So, as the world of post-quantum digital signature schemes evolve, and maybe Falcon doesn't win, maybe that's not the
standard people coalesce around. Um as other schemes become standardized and gain adoption, we'll be able to plug those in to our blockchain so that we
can be crypto agile as the entire industry adapts to the advancement of quantum computing. So, I've just barely scratched the surface of this post-quantum uh problem
and our solution to it. But, another one of my colleagues, Andrew Fank, he's going to be giving a talk at 2:00 p.m. today on stage 13. This is
downstairs in the city cube in the corner, right by the entrance. Uh he's going to be talking about this cryptographic agility and showing off
how to use Falcon signatures in TypeScript. Um so, you can make your way down there if you want to double click on this topic.
Um we'd love to have you there. And finally, if you have any questions uh that haven't already been submitted, the Algorand booth is right here to
stage left. I would love it if you would come by and chat with us. Feel free to to bring your questions, however difficult they may be. I I would love
some challenging questions on this topic. Um definitely come on by. We're doing demos throughout the day, and you can also sign up for a hackathon. We've
got cash prizes plus swag to give away throughout the expo. Cool. That's my story. >> [applause] >> Thank you very much, Brian. Uh two
questions for you. Uh our current rails don't support an agentic economy where agents create their own microeconomies and deal with millions of transactions per second,
potentially billions. Um how can we frame blockchain to support this without triggering people. Are there any other options besides blockchain? And that's from Andre
Andreu. >> Okay. So, uh there's a couple components to that question. One, I think there's a scale issue, right? With the growth of the agentic economy and blockchain
typically having limited capacity. One thing I'll say about that is there's a lot of available capacity on blockchains plural. Algorand can do an enormous

them. The other part of that question was are there other technologies? So, I sort of touched on this during the talk. The 402 status code is only intended to mean the
server is requesting some kind of payment. The X402 protocol is how the blockchain industry has rallied around that to say, "Here's how you can do it
with blockchain." Can you do it with other payment mechanisms? Yes. If you were to come up with a similar protocol that says, "My server accepts card
payments." or "My server accepts buy now, pay later." Like whatever it is, people could also form a standard around that and do payments in other ways. But
there's problems with that. There's costs, there's settlement times. And so, my initial premise that blockchain uniquely enables agentic commerce, I think is the bottom line from my
perspective. >> Okay. Uh one more question. What does payment simulation mean? Why is it required? >> Yeah, good question. So, in the Algorand workflow, we have a special capability
called simulate. This is just a node endpoint. Oh, it's not on the screen. Sorry. It's on my screen. So, Algorand nodes can fully simulate a transaction to see what will
happen without you having to submit it. So, this can be advantageous if you want to see like what are the fees right now that I would need to pay without
guessing. Um and there's other parameters that are hard to know at the time. Um and it also allows you to just evaluate every part of the transaction
without the risk that it goes through. So, it's like a safe way to dry run a transaction without actually submitting it. So, it gives you just another way to
work up to the moment that you submit the real thing and real money is going to exchange hands. Okay. So, that question was from Laszlo
Deak. >> Okay, Brian. >> Thank you. >> Thank you very much. >> My pleasure. >> Another round of applause for Brian, please. >> Thank you.
